item.title: US tells UN Houthis must cease attacks on Saudi, Yemeni governments
item.description:
US tells UN Houthis must cease attacks on Saudi, Yemeni governments

The United States Mission to the United Nations has called on the Houthis to stop their attacks "against the legitimate governments of Yemen and Saudi Arabia", while demanding that Iran end its support to the group

Speaking at a UN Security Council meeting on Yemen, Jeff Bartos, the US ambassador to the UN for Management and Reform, said: "The pattern is unmistakable: the terrorist Houthis act as instruments of Tehran to threaten freedom of navigation, undermine regional stability, and terrorise innocent civilians."

Bartos said the United States stood firmly with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government as they defend their sovereignty and work to restore stability.

The pattern is unmistakable: the terrorist Houthis act as instruments of Tehran to threaten freedom of navigation, undermine regional stability, and terrorize innocent civilians. We demand that the Houthis cease their attacks against the legitimate governments of Yemen and Saudi Arabia, and that Iran cease all support to the Houthis.

item.title: Yemeni government says 1,400 Houthis killed in 2,750 strikes
item.description:
Yemeni government says 1,400 Houthis killed in 2,750 strikes

Yemen's government has said more than 1,400 Houthi fighers were "neutralised" in more than 2,750 precision strikes its forces carried out during military operations over the past 24 hours.

Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili, the spokesperson for the armed forces, said the operations targeted high-value military assets deep within Houthi-held territory, according to a statement carried by Saba news agency.

The Yemeni government announced on Sunday the start of the operation “Dawn of Yemen” to retake Yemeni territory held by the Houthis.

item.title: Outrage grows over plan to livestream US military firing squad execution
item.description:
Outrage grows over plan to livestream US military firing squad execution

Condemnation of US plans for a public execution by military firing squad escalated Friday, as Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on whether it would be livestreamed as proposed and insisted he would not watch if it is.

Nidal Hasan's execution -- scheduled for December 3 at Fort Hood, Texas, where he gunned down 13 people in 2009 -- is set to be the first by US military firing squad since 1945.

Asked about the planned livestream, Vance told journalists he does not "know that that's actually going to happen."

"This is a guy who committed, in my view, the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11," Vance said, but added that if the execution is broadcast live, "I'm not going to be watching it."

Representative Austin Scott of President Donald Trump's Republican Party said he supported executing Hasan but "livestreaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that."

Senator Mark Kelly, a Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said Hasan should "face justice" but that public executions are "the kind of thing Iran and the Taliban do. Is this who we want to be associated with?"

A Pentagon official told AFP on Thursday that the execution would be streamed live, after US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said "we'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public."

But Trump on Friday contradicted Hegseth's confirmation, and said there has been no decision yet on whether to publicly broadcast the execution, which he supports.

"They are making a determination about that, but he will be killed," Trump said. "I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes."

The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights condemned the move, saying in a message sent to AFP on Friday that "the livestreaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture."

Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, said it was a "barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered."

Twelve of the 13 people Hasan killed and 30 of those he wounded were soldiers. He was shot by a civilian police officer who responded to the attack and is paralysed from the waist down.

Hasan chose to conduct his own defence during the trial but called no witnesses and gave no testimony, and made no attempt to deny the charges.

He was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013.

Court-appointed defence attorneys expressed concern that he was seeking execution.

The court that convicted Hasan was told he was opposed to the US military's occupations of Iraq and Afghanistan, and that he had spoken online with an alleged Al-Qaeda figure, Anwar al-Awlaki, an American citizen subsequently killed in a US drone strike in Yemen. 

Report by AFP

item.title: Trump welcomed Russia's involvement in Iran settlement efforts, Kremlin says
item.description:
Trump welcomed Russia's involvement in Iran settlement efforts, Kremlin says

The Kremlin has said US President Donald Trump welcomed Russia’s involvement in efforts aimed at reaching a settlement over Iran, Reuters reported.

Russian President Vladimir Putin and Trump spoke over a phone call on Friday, following which Trump said that Russia had agreed to immediately supply diesel to US and global markets in an effort to lower fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections next month.

Kremlin's comment comes a day after Putin told Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian that Moscow was ready to “do everything we can” to help end the war.

item.title: Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream execution puts US in dubious company
item.description:
Only Iran and Afghanistan routinely carry out sentences in public, with Saudi Arabia appearing to have ended practice

  • US politics – live updates

If the US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, goes ahead with plans to livestream the execution of a soldier radicalised to extremist Islam who killed 13 people at a military base in Texas, his country will join a motley assembly of lesser powers and rogue actors who have conducted public executions in recent years.

Only two countries currently systematically carry out capital sentences in public: Iran and Afghanistan. In 2025, the Taliban authorities carried out six such killings and the regime in Tehran 11, according to Amnesty International.
